summary: Before anyone lives on the Moon or Mars, crews, rovers and instruments are tested at "analog" sites on Earth. Those sites were mostly picked by tradition: places that were famous, easy to reach, or already had a research station. We wanted to know what happens if you let the data choose instead. Planetary Twin is an open web app that compares Earth's land with specific landing sites and base locations on the Moon and Mars, then shows the closest matches on an interactive globe. You choose a destination and what matters for your mission, and the map responds immediately. It confirms many of the sites scientists already use, and it points to promising places nobody has studied as analogs yet. It also tells you plainly where Earth cannot imitate another world at all. That matters because choosing the wrong test site wastes time and money, and choosing only familiar ones means better options stay hidden. Our tool makes the choice open, repeatable and available to any agency, researcher or student with a browser.
details: Planetary Twin is a web tool that helps mission planners and researchers find where on Earth scientifically resembles a specific place on the Moon or Mars. Every lunar and Martian mission rehearses on Earth first, but the sites used today were chosen over fifty years by reputation, road access and where a research station happened to be, nobody had asked the whole planet. So we scored all 341,040 land cells of a 0.25° global grid against 13 named regions, including Jezero Crater, Shackleton and Mare Tranquillitatis, across five dimensions: terrain, temperature, dryness, surface and atmosphere. You pick a region or mission profile, drag the weights, and the whole planet re-ranks live in your browser; every candidate site opens a field report showing what matches, what fails and the data behind each number. The analysis is a reproducible Python pipeline (NumPy, SciPy, Xarray, Rasterio) built only on public data that needs no login: LRO LOLA and Diviner, MGS MOLA and TES, MODIS, MERRA-2, GPM IMERG and CERES from NASA, plus NOAA ETOPO and the Mars Climate Database. The app is TypeScript, React and MapLibre GL, hosted on GitHub Pages, so it runs anywhere with no install. Our biggest challenge was that the first version ranked the Antarctic ice sheet first for everything; we fixed it by combining dimensions with a geometric mean, so a failed dimension cannot be averaged away. The method now recovers the sites scientists already trust: 11 of 13 established analog sites land in the top quarter of Earth's land, where chance would put about 3 (p ≈ 9 × 10⁻⁷), and the scoring code never sees those sites. It also found something new: Harrat Khaybar in Saudi Arabia matches Mare Tranquillitatis in 4 of 5 testable dimensions, sits in the top 0.05% of Earth's land, and has no previous analog study that we could find. We were strict about honesty: no place on Earth matches lunar or Martian temperature or atmosphere, and the app says so instead of hiding it. The impact is a faster, fairer and more transparent way to choose where crews, rovers and instruments are tested before launch, open to agencies and students alike. Next, we would add a fine-scale tier using 30 m elevation data and cross-check our results against independent JAXA datasets.
